To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

“Enteropathogenic E. coli cause diarrhea in children by adhering to the apical surface of the intestinal mucosa, inducing effacement of the microvilli, and causing a lesion in the apical cytoskeleton that is associated with the presence of bacteria.”
“Enteropathogenic Eschericia coli adhere to the small intestinal epithelium by a process of attaching and effacing, and this is the mechanism by which they cause diarrhea”.
enteropathogenic E. coli cause diarrhea in infants and young children by attaching to the intestinal mucosa and effacing the microvilli.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the pathogenesis of enteropathogenic Esch. coli (EPEC).
the pathogenicity of Escherichia colifrom the human gut.
enteropathogenic Es. coli and its interaction with intestinal mucosa, and the pathogenesis of diarrhea caused by enteropathogenic Esch. coli.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the enteropathogenic Esche- riche coli are a heterogeneous group of bacteria, which are able to adhere to the small intestinal epithelium and cause diarrhea by a process known as the attaching effacing phenomenon.

EPEC is the most important bacterial cause of infantile diarrhoea in the developing world, but that in the industrialized world it has been superseded by other pathogens, including rotavirus, noroviruses, and Campylobacter.

the enteropathogenic Escherechia coli is a pathogen that has been recognized as a major cause of diarrhea in children in developing countries and has been implicated in the pathogenesis of chronic diarrhea in children and travelers.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we had shown that the small intestinal mucosa was the site of the pathogenic action of enteropathogenic Esch. coli, and that this could be seen in the electron microscope as a lesion characterized by microvilli loss at sites of bacterial adhesions, and the presence of pedestals formed from apical membrane and cytoskeleton.
we identified the cause of the diarrhea, the attaching effacing mechanism of enteropathogenic Esch. coli, and that the diarrhea could be treated by a milk exclusion diet and intravenous antibiotics.

we were the first to demonstrate that enteropathogenic E coli adhered to the small intestinal mucosa and caused the attaching-effacing lesions, and that the lesion was associated with diarrhea in humans and in experimental animals.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we should not be afraid to use electron microscopy to study the causes of acute and chronic gastroenteritis.
the electron microscope is a useful tool for investigating intestinal disease.
the attaching-effacing lesions of enteropathogenic Esch. coli were the same in both children with chronic diarrhea, and children with acute gastroenteritis.
